records.name: Montenegro
records.summary:
Montenegro is workable for trans visitors — the Western Balkans' most advanced legal framework. It has a same-sex partnership law (2020), anti-discrimination law covering gender identity, and SOGI-inclusive hate-crime provisions; Podgorica Pride proceeds annually. Counterweights documented by ILGA-Europe: anti-LGBT and misogynistic hate speech in political rhetoric is a serious issue, and misdemeanour charges are overused in place of proper hate-crime prosecution (European Commission). There is no legal gender recognition law (administrative practice is inconsistent).

For a visitor: no legal exposure, functioning institutions, small tolerant coastal tourist scene; standard caution in the north.

sources.summary: ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2024 (covering 2023) chapter on Montenegro: anti-LGBT and misogynistic hate speech and political rhetoric continued; a psychologist wearing non-gender-conforming clothes on TV was targeted by hate comments, threats and several physical attacks (police response monitored); a groundbreaking study found only 28.1% of companies' anti-discrimination policies explicitly mention sexual orientation; a new Action Plan for the 2019-2023 LGBTI Strategy was adopted with €45,000; over 222 online hate-speech incidents reported.

Human Dignity Trust global legal history (updated 18 June 2026): Montenegro appears among the 1977 European decriminalisations (Croatia/Slovenia/Montenegro cohort); reference source for MNE's decriminalisation date rather than MNE-specific analysis.

GlobalGayz (March 2012): decriminalised in 1977; small gay scene with deeply entrenched anti-gay opinion, discrimination and harassment when visible; the first Podgorica Pride was cancelled in May 2011 after two attacks on gay people in the capital. Dated but concrete on social climate.

Al Jazeera (Oct 2013): Montenegro's first Pride marched through Podgorica — roughly 150 marchers guarded by some 2,000 police, rock-throwing opponents stopped by tear gas; Queer Montenegro's Danijel Kalezic: 'From this day we are no longer invisible.' Shows both state protection and organised hostility.

PinkNews (2 Aug 2019): MPs blocked the same-sex partnership law on 31 July 2019 despite government backing — ERA's Western Balkans office: LGBT people 'forced to live as second-class citizens' (no hospital visitation or shared-benefit rights); a 2018 ERA study found 51% of LGBT+ Montenegrins were closeted.

CDM (Dec 2018): the Government adopted the Draft Law on Same-Sex Partnership granting couples near marriage-equivalent rights via registrar ceremony — explicitly excluding parenting, foster care and adoption; shows the reform trajectory before the 2019 parliamentary block.

records.name: Bosnia and Herzegovina
records.summary:
Bosnia and Herzegovina is workable for trans visitors. Nothing is criminalised; the capital Sarajevo’s Pride has proceeded annually since 2019 with heavy (necessary) police protection; and most cantons have now appointed prosecutors specifically for anti-LGBTI hate crimes — genuine institutional progress.

Counterweights from the 2024 Pink Report (the annual monitor): negative events are accumulating, the trend is unfavourable outside Sarajevo (especially in one internal region, Republika Srpska), and trans people occupy a “precarious position” — no legal gender recognition framework, restricted healthcare access, and institutional suspicion. The state is also deeply dysfunctional generally.

For a visitor: no legal exposure; stick to Sarajevo and tourist areas; avoid visible trans presentation in the hostile internal region (Republika Srpska) and rural areas. Marriage recognition is restricted to opposite-sex couples in the entities — relevant to same-sex partners travelling together; the border and document position for visitors is not detailed in the current sources.<

sources.summary: Sarajevo Open Centre, Pink Report 2024 (13 Jun 2024): annual report on LGBTI human rights in Bosnia and Herzegovina — the past year saw a number of negative events with significant impact, and the long-visible worsening trend is 'becoming increasingly evident'. For this record: current national climate assessment from the leading local monitor.

Balkan Diskurs (25 Oct 2024): legal gender recognition is formally accessible but vague and ineffective in practice — the Council of Ministers' 2022 action plan conditions document changes on 'completed' medical transition, constraints described as discriminatory and degrading. For this record: the documentation pathway a trans person navigating the system faces — resident-facing, not a border issue.

Human Rights Watch (4 Feb 2014): violent attack on Sarajevo Pride organisers — Sarajevo Open Centre staff said they had arranged security with police about three weeks earlier; HRW's Lydia Gall demanded prosecution of attackers. For this record: precedent that organised anti-LGBT violence occurs even WITH prior police coordination (dated 2014, context for later attacks).

GlobalGayz (2012): same-sex conduct decriminalised in the Federation of BiH (1996) and Republika Srpska (1998) via the two entities' own criminal codes; the 2009 Law Against Discrimination prohibits discrimination on sexual orientation but omitted gender identity as originally intended. For this record: entity-level legal baseline plus the pre-2016 gender-identity protection gap.

Sarajevo Open Centre (Jul 2016): BiH's amended Anti-Discrimination Law explicitly covers sexual orientation and gender identity with correct local terminology — SOC co-presented the amendments with the Agency for Gender Equality after fall-2015 public consultations. For this record: the statutory protection now on the books at state level.

Sarajevo Open Centre (Jul 2016): the Federation of BiH adopted hate-crime regulation explicitly naming sexual orientation and gender identity as aggravating circumstances — SOC coordinator Vladana Vasić confirming the long-sought coalition win. For this record: entity-level sentencing enhancement for bias attacks in FBiH (RS runs its own separate regime).
